subtitle: Multi-agent teamwork on a real domain: role design, task delegation, tools, and hand-offs for catalog, pricing, and support crews — CrewAI in an e-commerce context
audience: Developers who finished LangGraph for E-commerce (graphs, state, routers, HITL) and now split work across specialized agents instead of one graph. Team mechanics are taught as runnable JS miniatures in the playground; production shapes target real CrewAI (Python) with accurate Agent/Task/Crew APIs.
outcomes: Decide single-graph vs multi-agent by coordination needs, and draw the boundary explicitly
Write roles (role/goal/backstory) with non-overlapping mandates and testable scopes
Specify tasks with expected outputs and context passing that prevent rework
Run sequential crews for fixed pipelines with stage contracts and replay
Run hierarchical crews with manager delegation, budgets, and termination proofs
Design handoff protocols and shared task boards that prevent dropped and duplicated work
Scope tools per role (least privilege) with selection tests
Evaluate teams per-agent and end-to-end with blame attribution across agents
Diagnose team failure modes: role drift, delegation loops, context bloat, agent conflicts
Ship a marketplace crew: catalog + pricing + support agents measured on a gold set

assessment.q: Single graph vs agent team for fixed triage→decide→draft. Choice?
options: Single graph/chain: fixed pipeline with no coordination needs — teams pay coordination overhead for zero benefit
assessment.explain: Teams cost coordination (handoff formats, delegation logic, compounded errors). Pay it only for variable, specialized, or parallelizable work (Ch.1).

assessment.q: Two roles both 'ensure quality'. Predict the failure?
options: Overlapping mandates: duplicated work plus diffusion of responsibility — scopes must partition the job with testable boundaries
assessment.explain: Role design partitions accountability. Overlap duplicates effort and lets failures fall between owners (Ch.2).

options: Agents improvise formats — downstream parsing breaks; expected outputs are contracts, not suggestions
assessment.explain: Handoffs need shapes: without expected outputs each agent invents formats and the next stage chokes. Contracts per task (Ch.3).

assessment.q: Sequential crew for catalog (research→write→review). When does it break?
options: When steps need skipping/reordering by judgment (conditional flows) — then hierarchical/supervisor routing
assessment.explain: Sequential fits fixed pipelines; conditional work needs dynamic delegation. Topology follows variability (Ch.4, LangGraph Ch.8).

assessment.q: Hierarchical crew loops researcher→writer→researcher forever. Missing?
options: Termination: max rounds + done-flag, same proof supervisors need — unbounded delegation hangs
assessment.explain: Dynamic delegation cycles without bounds. Caps + completion criteria are structural, not optional (Ch.5).

assessment.q: Two agents both email the customer about one ticket. Root cause + fix?
options: Handoff gap: no claimed ownership on the shared board — tasks need claim/complete states with exactly one owner
assessment.explain: Unowned shared work duplicates (or drops when each assumes the other). Task boards with ownership states prevent both (Ch.6).

assessment.q: Support agent holds the refund-issue tool. Verdict?
options: Least-privilege violation: support drafts, finance-team tools execute — scope tools per role and test selection
assessment.explain: Tool scope follows role authority: drafting ≠ executing. Over-tooled agents cause out-of-mandate actions (Ch.7).

assessment.q: Team fails end-to-end but each agent passes unit checks. Missing layer?
options: Team gold runs with per-agent attribution: handoffs, delegation choices, and shared-state reads under composition
assessment.explain: Composition creates emergent failures (dropped handoffs, misdelegation). End-to-end runs with blame attribution catch integration truth (Ch.8).

assessment.q: Reviewer agent starts rewriting instead of reviewing. Name + fix?
options: Role drift: mandate and output contract re-asserted (review → verdict + fixes list, never rewritten copy), with drift gold items
assessment.explain: Roles decay toward generic helpfulness without enforced outputs. Contracts + drift tests hold mandates (Ch.9).

assessment.q: Context grows 3x per added agent. Control?
options: Summarized handoffs (decisions + open items, not transcripts) plus per-role minimal context — share conclusions, not histories
assessment.explain: Handoff bloat compounds per agent. Summarized, minimal, referenced context scales teams; transcript-passing doesn't (Ch.9).

assessment.q: Pricing agent needs live competitor data mid-run. Pattern?
options: Tool with validated args + fresh-data timestamp in handoffs (staleness visible downstream)
assessment.explain: Live data enters through scoped tools; timestamps make freshness auditable downstream. Stale prices need visible age, not silent reuse (Ch.7 + capstone).

assessment.q: v2 team beats v1 overall, regresses VIP handling. Ship?
options: No: per-segment no-regression gate — fix VIP path first (same discipline as single-graph eval)
assessment.explain: Segment gates transfer unchanged to teams: localized regressions never ship on averages (Ch.8 + capstone).

project.title: The Marketplace Crew
project.summary: Ship a three-crew marketplace team (catalog, pricing, support) with designed roles, contracted tasks, tested delegation, scoped tools, and a gold-set evaluation with per-segment diffs. The multi-agent capstone: teams measured like systems, not demoed like magic.
requirements: Role cards: role/goal/backstory/tools for 5+ agents with non-overlap justification per pair of neighbors
Task specs: expected outputs + context-passing contracts for every handoff in the pipeline
Topology decision: sequential vs hierarchical per crew with the variability argument recorded
Tool scoping: per-role toolsets with least-privilege rationale; refund execution outside support's scope
Gold runs: 12 conversations (happy/edge/attack) with terminal paths, per-agent attribution, and no-regression gate
Operations: delegation budgets, termination proofs, handoff board design, refusal/skip audit plan
technical: Team machinery in runnable JS miniatures (runner, board, router, attribution) plus real CrewAI Python shapes
All handoffs schema-shaped; all tools closed-schema with outcome routing
Threads/boards namespaced per crew; no cross-crew state leakage
Numbers reproducible: gold set + routing/delegation tests committed
project.architecture: Four sections: (1) Team chart — roles, mandates, topology per crew with variability arguments; (2) Runs — traced conversations per crew with per-agent attribution; (3) Evaluation — gold scores, per-segment diffs, iterated fix with delta; (4) Operations — budgets, termination proofs, board design, guardrails.
steps: Write role cards with overlap analysis before any code
Specify tasks with expected outputs; build the handoff board
Implement crews per topology decision; test delegation branches
Scope tools per role; verify selection with adversarial picks
Run gold set; attribute failures per agent; iterate one variable; re-score
Write operations section; self-review against Ch.9 failure gallery
evaluation: Role mandates partition without overlap (pairwise justification present)
Every handoff contracted and tested; board states cover claim/complete/skip
Delegation branches covered including fallback; loops termination-proved
Gold baseline + iteration with per-segment diffs on the same set
Refund execution outside support scope, proven by toolset audit
stretch: Add a fraud-review crew composed as a subgraph with its own gold items
Instrument delegation budgets (max rounds/depth) with overrun alerts
Convert one sequential crew to hierarchical and report measured trade-offs

interviewQs.q: Single agent vs team — how do you decide?
interviewQs.a: By coordination needs: fixed pipeline with no branching judgment → single graph/chain. Variable delegation across specialties, parallelizable research, or distinct authority domains (pricing vs support) → team. Cost the coordination explicitly (handoff formats, delegation logic, compounded error rates, context growth) against the specialization gain — and revisit when the topology's variability changes.

interviewQs.q: What makes a good agent role card?
interviewQs.a: Role (identity), goal (measurable outcome it owns), backstory (domain context shaping judgment), tools (least-privilege set), and non-overlap with neighbors (pairwise justification). Testable scope beats colorful persona: the card must predict what the agent will and won't touch. Review cards for mandate collisions before any code — overlap found in review is cheap, in production expensive.

interviewQs.q: How do agents hand off without dropping or duplicating work?
interviewQs.a: Shared task board with ownership states (open → claimed → done/skipped), exactly one owner per task, contracted output shapes at handoff, and idempotent consumers (re-runs safe). Claim-before-work prevents duplication; completion receipts prevent drops; skip reasons preserve auditability. Handoff protocol is tested like an API: claim races, skip paths, malformed outputs.

interviewQs.q: Manager keeps delegating in circles. Fix?
interviewQs.a: Termination by construction: max delegation rounds + done-flag criteria checked per loop, with the manager's own routing tests covering exit branches. Then diagnose why exits never triggered (unclear completion criteria vs genuinely hard task) — caps stop the bleeding, criteria fix the cause. Loops without proofs are hangs awaiting traffic.

interviewQs.q: Support agent issued a refund directly. Postmortem?
interviewQs.a: Least-privilege failure: execution tools lived in a drafting role's scope. Fix: remove issuance from support's toolset (draft + recommend only), route execution through approval-gated finance path, add toolset audit to review checklist, and add a gold attack item (refund-pressure ticket) asserting no direct issuance. Blame the scope design, not the agent.

interviewQs.q: Team passes agent unit tests, fails customers. Evaluation gap?
interviewQs.a: Missing composition layer: end-to-end conversation gold sets with per-agent attribution (which handoff/delegation/state-read failed), run on every change with per-segment no-regression gates. Unit tests verify parts; gold runs verify teamwork — handoffs, delegation choices, and shared-state reads only exist in composition.
